Neonates of the mountain goat are born with a wet weight at birth of approximately 3200 grams [Wwb = approximately 3200 grams], a mass that represents a significant maternal investment given the rugged alpine terrain they will soon navigate. This neonatal mass is relatively substantial for a caprine species of this size, providing the newborn with essential energy reserves for thermoregulation and early locomotion in steep, rocky habitats. Under the core body temperature typical for this species, which is maintained at 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], female kids achieve an adult body mass of 73,000 grams [Wwi = 73,000 grams], while males attain a considerably larger ultimate wet weight of 105,000 grams [Wwi = 105,000 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with males outweighing females by more than forty percent, is thought to reflect the intense intrasexual competition among males for access to receptive females during the breeding season. The disparity in adult body mass also influences habitat use and foraging behavior, with larger males often able to exploit higher-quality forage patches that smaller individuals cannot defend.

The gestation period in mountain goats lasts for 184 days [tg = 184 days], a duration that has been confirmed through longitudinal studies of tagged females in the Rocky Mountains at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This relatively extended gestation, occurring under the species' normal physiological temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], aligns with the production of a single well-developed precocial calf that is capable of following its mother within hours of birth. Following parturition, the offspring enters a period of nutritional dependence characterized by intensive suckling. The time since birth at weaning has been documented at 122 days [tx = 122 days], a milestone that marks the transition to a diet dominated by alpine grasses, sedges, and forbs at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This weaning age is relatively protracted compared to some other alpine ungulates, likely reflecting the slow growth rates imposed by the low-quality forage available at high elevations and the need for extensive maternal guidance in learning complex foraging and predator-avoidance behaviors.

Reproductive output in the mountain goat is modest when compared to many other bovids, with females giving birth to a single calf per litter in the vast majority of recorded cases [N_R_i = single calf per litter in the vast majority of recorded cases]. This low litter size is compensated for by consistent annual breeding, as females typically produce one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year] under favorable nutritional conditions. The maximum reproductive rate, therefore, equates to 1.2 calves per year when the small proportion of twin births is accounted for, a value measured at the species' core body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This conservative reproductive strategy is characteristic of long-lived mammals inhabiting unpredictable and resource-limited environments, where the energetic cost of gestation and lactation is substantial, and where investing in a single, high-quality offspring each season maximizes lifetime fitness over repeated breeding attempts.

Sexual maturation in the mountain goat is a gradual process that unfolds across several years of sub-adult life in the alpine environment. The time since birth at puberty has been estimated at 912 days [tp = 912 days] in females, a stage that coincides with the onset of estrous cycling and the ability to conceive, though actual first parturition is often deferred until the individual has attained sufficient body mass at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This pubertal milestone, assessed at the standard mammalian core temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], is reached considerably later than in many lowland ungulates of comparable body size. The prolonged juvenile and sub-adult period allows young mountain goats to acquire critical survival skills, including navigating treacherous cliff faces to escape predators such as wolves and golden eagles, and building the fat reserves necessary to withstand the severe winter conditions that characterize their high-elevation habitat. Males tend to mature slightly later than females.

Longevity in the mountain goat is remarkable for a medium-sized ungulate inhabiting a harsh, energetically demanding environment. The maximum documented lifespan in the wild has been recorded at 20.8 years [am = 20.8 years], a figure determined through long-term mark-recapture studies of known individuals in protected populations at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This impressive lifespan, measured under the species' normal physiological temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], reflects a life-history strategy characterized by high adult survival, low reproductive output per breeding event, and delayed sexual maturation. The capacity for extended survival is supported by several key adaptations, including a dense, insulating winter coat, a slow metabolic rate relative to body mass, and exceptionally well-developed social hierarchies that reduce the risk of fatal intraspecific aggression. Comparative data from other caprids suggest that this longevity places the mountain goat among the longest-lived members of its subfamily, a pattern consistent with the slow pace of life that typifies large-bodied, high-latitude herbivores.
